newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No snail's pace growth for Belgium's Floridienne.
newsitem.headline: No snail's pace growth for Belgium's Floridienne.

text.p: Belgian holding company Floridienne, founded 99 years ago on slave labour but now motoring comfortably on a diet of snails, metal residues and billiard balls, had a good year in 1996 and sees more in 1997.
"Things are going well," a beaming company President Jean-Marie Delwart told reporters presenting the company's final 1996 figures on Thursday.

Floridienne clocked up a 35 percent rise in net profits to 121.9 million francs in calendar 1996 against 90.2 million in the previous 12 months on a turnover up to 2.7 billion francs from 2.4 billion.
The company, still majority owned by the descendants of the families who founded it in 1898 to dig for phosphates in Florida, is now divided into four main divisions.
The agri-food division majors in edible snails from Eastern Europe, while the residual metals division is increasingly focused on recycling cadmium and nickel batteries.
Floridienne also has a substantial minority stake in holding company Berginvest which, among other things, is a leading world manufacturer of billiard balls.
The fourth, and newest division, is the venture capital section which takes stakes in small niche-market companies -- particularly in Eastern Europe and Africa.
The turnover of the Floragro division rose to 1.5 billion francs last year from 1.5 billion in 1995, and profits climbed to 55.9 million francs from 38.0 million.
"When we started in snails it was badly received by the banks," Delwart said. "Happily the snails are going very well."
He said the company had snail interests in countries ranging from Romania to Poland, Albania, Turkey and Ukraine.
Delwart said the agri-food division was actively looking at delving into black truffles, black pepper and seafood.
"We should achieve some of this in the next three months," he added.
He described the company's residual metals division, Floridienne Chimie, as "the rag and bone merchants" of the sector, being the first in the world to have a cadmium battery recycling plant.
It was also interested in the thousands of tonnes of zinc oxide batteries that are thrown away each year in Europe.
The division's profits climbed to 24.3 million francs last year from 17.2 million in 1996 on a turnover up to 1.2 billion francs from 1.1 billion.

Income from the 23.4 percent stake in Berginvest fell last year to 25.1 million francs from 40.5 million as the company's own income fell. But Floridienne booked a 21.4 million profit on the sale of four percent of Berginvest's shares.
Florinvest, Delwart said, had made some interesting investments last year including a small company developing chemical receptors that could latch onto viruses and neutralise them.
It was also interested in developing what he termed chemical mobile phones or, in other words communication via chemical signals.
"We are studying the language of chemicals," Delwart said. "There are lots of possibilities."
